hook: Two stores raise prices by 10% on the same day. The gas station on the highway barely notices: drivers still fill up. The sparkling water brand at the supermarket loses a third of its sales overnight, because five other brands sit on the same shelf. How strongly buyers respond to a price is a number you can calculate.

ideas: Price elasticity of demand = percent change in quantity demanded divided by percent change in price. Read the absolute value.
Greater than 1: elastic. Less than 1: inelastic. Exactly 1: unit elastic. Zero: perfectly inelastic (vertical). Infinite: perfectly elastic (horizontal).
Total revenue test: elastic demand, price and TR move opposite; inelastic demand, they move together; unit elastic, TR does not change.
Along a straight-line demand curve the slope is constant but elasticity is not: elastic at the top, unit elastic at the midpoint, inelastic at the bottom.
Demand is more elastic with close substitutes, a large budget share, a narrowly defined good and more time to adjust.

misconception.wrong: An elasticity of $-0.4$ is negative, so demand is elastic; a steeper curve is always the less elastic one.
misconception.right: Judge elasticity by the absolute value: 0.4 is less than 1, so demand is inelastic. And slope is not elasticity: one straight-line demand curve has the same slope everywhere but is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low ones.

summary: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded responds to a price change: the percent change in quantity over the percent change in price, read as an absolute value. Above 1 demand is elastic, below 1 inelastic, at 1 unit elastic. The total revenue test follows: with elastic demand a price rise lowers total revenue, with inelastic demand it raises it. Close substitutes, a large budget share and more time to adjust make demand more elastic.
